newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Russian differences with NATO hang over summit.
newsitem.headline: Russian differences with NATO hang over summit.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
A European security summit hoping to lay the foundations of peace for the 21st century opens on Monday, but with another row looming between Russia and the West over NATO expansion.

Leaders from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) will approve plans for shoring up peace in Bosnia, set a new course for arms control and discuss problems such as the crisis in Belarus at the two-day summit.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin signalled he would take a tough line on plans by the Western alliance to take in new members from Eastern Europe -- an issue which has already disrupted efforts to build a new age of cooperation in the post-Cold War world.
"We are categorically against the expansion of NATO to the East," Chernomyrdin said before he flew to Lisbon. "Russia has its position and will stand by it at the OSCE meeting."

President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, is not coming to the summit and has sent Chernomyrdin instead. Russia says it will be isolated and threatened if countries like Poland and Hungary join the Western alliance.
Western diplomats say they would prefer the Lisbon summit, which brings together the United States and Canada with European states, to avoid the debate on NATO enlargement.
The last OSCE summit two years ago in Budapest was wrecked by a row over the same issue and by differences over Bosnia.

As other leaders arrived in Lisbon for the meeting, a senior U.S. official told reporters Washington saw the OSCE and NATO as working together and said the summit was "not a debate about NATO enlargement".
Leaders will issue a declaration in Lisbon committing them to develop a security blueprint for the continent.

"As we approach the new century, it is more important than ever that we build together a peaceful...region where all our nations and individuals feel secure," reads the declaration, a draft of which was obtained by Reuters.

Russia has found little support for its efforts to go further and develop the OSCE into a more powerful institution that would act as a counterbalance to NATO. Moscow has insisted the summit must not appear to endorse the alliance's plans.

Western nations, and Eastern European countries which are queuing up to join NATO, oppose any measures which would limit their freedom. The United States -- represented by Vice President Al Gore when he flies in from Washington for just a few hours on Monday -- has taken a tough line on this.
Diplomats said the summit declaration would endorse the general right of countries to join alliances, but without mentioning NATO so as to avoid any direct offence to Moscow.
Officials spent Sunday trying to reach final agreement on the summit documents, with debates on issues ranging from ethnic conflicts to arms control expected to last deep into the night.
One year after the end of the war in Bosnia, the meeting will agree a continued role for the OSCE there, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force.
The OSCE organised September's elections in Bosnia, has overseen an arms control agreement for former Yugoslavia and monitored human rights and democratic freedoms in the region.

Bosnia and Croatia will attend the summit but the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro was suspended from the OSCE in 1992. The political turmoil in Serbia, with thousands demonstrating in the streets, is likely to be another focus.

Leaders will also agree that a new round of arms talks should start in Vienna next year to cut military hardware in Europe, adapting and expanding a 1990 treaty signed between NATO and the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

Russia has insisted the treaty should be adapted to reflect the new security situation and is currently negotiating hard on the details. The West hopes this will go some way to reassuring Moscow that NATO does not pose a threat.
Many leaders are expected to voice concern about developments in Belarus, where President Alexander Lukashenko has strengthened his grip on power in a recent referendum.

Born in 1975 in Helsinki as a forum for discussing issues from democracy to economics, the European security body was sidelined until the end of the Cold War but has taken on an increasingly important role now that the East-West divide has gone.
